title: Equal-revenue tax reforms have strictly different worker burdens
scope: Global revenue and worker-welfare comparative statics in the source's small-open-economy Cobb-Douglas tax benchmark.
significance: Proves the exact Laffer peak, strict global monotonicity of normalized incidence and worker compensation, and a strict burden ranking for equal-revenue reforms.
body:
# Equal-revenue tax reforms have strictly different worker burdens

The open-economy theorem's incidence formula admits a global comparison that is useful when revenue is the policy target. Two positive tax rates raising the same revenue generally impose different domestic worker burdens. The higher-rate reform is strictly worse for workers for every recycling fraction allowed by the source.

Keep \(0<\alpha<1\), \(a=\alpha/(1-\alpha)\), \(g\in[0,1]\), and baseline output \(Y_0>0\). The source gives
\[
T(\tau)=\alpha Y_0\tau(1-\tau)^a,\quad
CV(\tau)=(1-\alpha)Y_0[1-(1-\tau)^a]-gT(\tau).
\tag{A}
\]
The domain is \(0<\tau<1\), with the baseline at zero.

First, receipts have exactly one peak:
\[
T'(\tau)=\alpha Y_0(1-\tau)^{a-1}[1-(a+1)\tau].
\]
Thus the maximizing rate is \(\tau^*=1/(a+1)=1-\alpha\), and
\[
T_{\max}=\alpha(1-\alpha)Y_0\alpha^a.
\tag{B}
\]
Receipts increase strictly before \(\tau^*\), decrease strictly afterward, and converge to zero at either end. Continuity and these strict inequalities imply that every target \(t\in(0,T_{\max})\) has exactly two implementing rates \(\tau_L<\tau^*<\tau_H\). The peak has exactly one rate; targets above the peak are infeasible in this benchmark.

For the two rates implementing the same positive target, transfers \(gt\) cancel from the compensation difference:
\[
CV(\tau_H)-CV(\tau_L)
=(1-\alpha)Y_0[(1-\tau_L)^a-(1-\tau_H)^a]>0.
\tag{C}
\]
Dividing by the common \(t\) proves the same strict ranking for incidence. The sign does not require estimating or fixing a special recycling fraction: it holds for each common \(g\). Economically, equal receipts imply equal transfers, while the high-rate equilibrium has lower capital, output and wage income.

A stronger property is that compensation itself is strictly increasing throughout the positive-rate domain. Direct differentiation gives
\[
CV'(\tau)=\alpha Y_0(1-\tau)^{a-1}
\{(1-g)(1-\tau)+ga\tau\}>0.
\tag{D}
\]
At \(g=0\) the first summand is strictly positive; at \(g=1\) the second is strictly positive; intermediate values preserve positivity. Complete recycling therefore does not reverse the global welfare ranking, even on the decreasing-revenue branch. At zero its first derivative vanishes when \(g=1\), consistently with the manuscript's second-order distortion.

Normalized incidence is also strictly increasing. Set \(f(\tau)=(1-\tau)^{-a}\). Equation (1) in the source is
\[
\iota(\tau)+g=\frac{f(\tau)-f(0)}{a\tau}
=\frac1{a\tau}\int_0^\tau f'(s)\,ds.
\]
Because \(f'\) is strictly increasing, its average over \([0,\tau]\) increases strictly as the upper endpoint increases. This proves monotonicity without a fragile sign expansion. The lower limit is \(1-g\); as \(\tau\uparrow1\), incidence diverges to infinity while compensation converges to the finite lost baseline wage bill \((1-\alpha)Y_0\). The divergence comes from the vanishing denominator \(T(\tau)\), not from an unbounded household loss.

These are conditional global comparative statics, not an empirical tax-rate recommendation. They hold with perfectly elastic foreign capital supply, quasilinear domestic workers who own no capital, fixed labor and the specified revenue use. The source's fixed-capital redistribution and announcement-wealth propositions concern different environments and are not combined with (A). No external references or actual ownership and mobility parameters are verified.

title: Sparse implementation: one randomized group under one funding constraint
scope: Structural refinement of the finite-group microcredit oracle and its quadratic aggregate-displacement extension.
significance: Proves existence of an oracle randomizing in at most one group, and at most two groups with aggregate uptake fixed, with a sharp one-group example.
body:
# Sparse implementation under funding and uptake constraints

The manuscript permits budget-induced randomization but does not bound how much randomization is needed. Its finite-group oracle has a particularly simple implementation: there always exists an optimum assigning deterministic offers in every group except possibly one. This remains true with multiple offers per group. In the quadratic scale model, at most two groups need randomize.

Include no offer explicitly as action zero, with \(\tau_{j0}=c_{j0}=0\), and write \(x_{ja}\) for action probabilities, so
\[
x_{ja}\ge0,\qquad \sum_{a=0}^Ax_{ja}=1,\qquad
\sum_{j,a}p_jc_{ja}x_{ja}\le B.
\tag{A}
\]
The objective is \(\sum p_j\tau_{ja}x_{ja}\). The source's assumptions ensure that this is a nonempty compact polytope; a linear objective attains its maximum at an extreme point.

At an extreme point with a binding budget, there are at most \(J+1\) positive coordinates. To see this directly, suppose more coordinates are positive. Restrict the \(J\) group-sum equations and the budget equality to these coordinates. Their matrix has rank at most \(J+1\), so a nonzero vector \(z\) is in its nullspace. For sufficiently small \(\epsilon>0\), both \(x+\epsilon z\) and \(x-\epsilon z\) remain nonnegative, preserve all group sums and preserve the budget. They are distinct feasible points with midpoint \(x\), a contradiction.

Every group requires at least one positive coordinate. Therefore at most one group can have two positive coordinates, and no group can have three. All other groups receive a single action with probability one. If the budget is slack, the same perturbation argument uses only the \(J\) group equations: sufficiently small perturbations preserve the strict budget inequality, giving at most \(J\) positive coordinates. Thus a slack-budget extreme optimum is entirely deterministic.

This is an existence statement, not a claim that every optimal policy is sparse. Ties can make convex combinations of sparse optima optimal and produce randomization in many groups. A degenerate budget row may also lower the available rank; it cannot invalidate the upper bound.

The one-group exception is necessary. Take one group and one nonzero action with cost one and welfare gain one, with \(0<B<1\). The policy's offer probability must satisfy \(x\le B\), and its value is \(x\), so the unique optimum is \(x=B\). It randomizes between the offer and no offer, while every deterministic feasible policy has value zero. This example satisfies the source's cost and welfare bounds.

Now consider the source's scaled welfare
\[
\mathcal V(x)=V(x)-\eta Q(x)^2/2,\qquad
Q(x)=\sum_{j,a}p_jd_{ja}x_{ja},
\]
with \(d_{j0}=0\). Choose any optimum and denote its aggregate uptake by \(q^*\). On the slice \(Q=q^*\), maximizing \(\mathcal V\) is exactly maximizing the linear objective \(V\), because the quadratic term is constant. Choose an extreme-point maximizer of this sliced polytope. It remains globally optimal: a higher value on the slice would contradict the original optimum.

The positive-coordinate argument now has the group equations, one uptake equality and, if binding, one budget equality. Hence there exists an optimum with at most \(J+2\) positive coordinates. At most two groups randomize; if both do, each uses two actions. Alternatively one group may use three. If the budget is slack, the upper bound improves to \(J+1\), so at most one group randomizes. Redundant uptake or budget rows can further reduce these bounds.

The argument applies to the declared population-probability optimization, not a guarantee about realized finite-portfolio spending. It does not identify the uptake externality parameter or transport trial effects across markets. It supports the source's oracle characterization and gives an implementable structural refinement without claiming a solution to private-type contract design.

title: Exact productivity directions and sharper nonlinear network error certificates
scope: Fixed-link CES price equilibrium: invariance, signed curvature comparison and a shock-residual refinement of the uniform error bound.
significance: Identifies a nonzero exact shock direction for arbitrary CES elasticities and proves a strictly sharper computable error bound after removing that direction.
body:
# Exact productivity directions and sharper network error certificates

The uniform approximation theorem is valid, but its bound can be sharpened by exploiting an exact direction of the nonlinear equilibrium. A shock proportional to the vector of primary-factor shares produces an exactly common log-price change, regardless of the intermediate substitution elasticities.

Use the source's notation \(a=(a_i)\), \(F\), \(A_{ij}=(1-a_i)b_{ij}\), \(\rho=\max_i(1-a_i)<1\), and \(M=\max_i(1-a_i)|r_i|\). Let \(x(\varepsilon)\) be its unique equilibrium and \(x^{\rm lin}(\varepsilon)=(I-A)^{-1}\varepsilon\). For every real \(c\),
\[
F(x+c\mathbf1)=F(x)+c(\mathbf1-a).
\tag{A}
\]
For \(r_i\ne0\), factor \(e^{r_ic}\) out of the sum defining \(F_i\); for \(r_i=0\), the displayed equality follows from the row sum. This proves (A) for every source technology.

Consequently
\[
x(\varepsilon+ca)=x(\varepsilon)+c\mathbf1.
\tag{B}
\]
Indeed substitution using (A) verifies the fixed-point equation, and uniqueness completes the proof. Since \((I-A)\mathbf1=a\), the same shift identity holds for the linear approximation. Their difference is therefore invariant under adding \(ca\) to the shock vector.

Apply the manuscript's uniform theorem to \(\varepsilon-ca\), then use (B). This gives the improved certificate
\[
\|x(\varepsilon)-x^{\rm lin}(\varepsilon)\|_\infty
\le\frac{M}{2(1-\rho)^3}
\left(\min_{c\in\mathbb R}\|\varepsilon-ca\|_\infty\right)^2.
\tag{C}
\]
The minimum exists because every \(a_i>0\), making the residual norm tend to infinity with \(|c|\). It is never larger than the original shock norm, since \(c=0\) is feasible. It can be zero for a nonzero shock: if \(\varepsilon=ca\), both exact and linear prices equal \(c\mathbf1\). This substantially distinguishes network-relative shocks from common price movements.

The scalar minimization is itself explicit as an interval-feasibility problem. A candidate residual radius \(E\ge0\) is feasible exactly when
\[
\max_i\frac{\varepsilon_i-E}{a_i}
\le
\min_i\frac{\varepsilon_i+E}{a_i}.
\]
This follows by solving \(|\varepsilon_i-ca_i|\le E\) for each \(c\) and intersecting the intervals. Thus (C) does not require solving another nonlinear equilibrium.

One can additionally determine the direction of the price error when elasticities are on the same side of one. The manuscript's Hessian formula shows that \(F_i\) is convex when \(r_i\ge0\) and concave when \(r_i\le0\). Because \(F_i(0)=0\) and \(DF(0)=A\), all \(r_i\ge0\) imply \(F(x)\ge Ax\) coordinatewise. Therefore
\[
x-x^{\rm lin}=(I-A)^{-1}[F(x)-Ax]\ge0,
\]
using the inverse's nonnegative Neumann series. If all \(r_i\le0\), the inequality reverses. This holds for signed shocks as well as adverse shocks. If signs differ, no uniform coordinatewise ranking follows from this argument.

For equal primary shares \(a_i=a_0\), there is a further dispersion bound. Every \(F_i(x)\) lies between \((1-a_0)\min_jx_j\) and \((1-a_0)\max_jx_j\). Thus \({\rm osc}(x)\le{\rm osc}(\varepsilon)/(1-\rho)\). The variance bound \({\rm Var}(x_j)\le{\rm osc}(x)^2/4\), inserted into the source's Taylor proof, gives
\[
\|x-x^{\rm lin}\|_\infty
\le\frac{M\,{\rm osc}(\varepsilon)^2}{8(1-\rho)^3}.
\]
For one sector the dispersion vanishes and exactness follows as expected.

These are analytical refinements of the fixed-link price benchmark. They do not extend smoothness through inventory depletion or endogenous link changes, and they do not equate gross output with welfare or value added. No computational or empirical reproduction is claimed.
